Every power deal in Africa has a day on which everyone in the room agrees it has succeeded.

The loan agreements are signed. The first drawdown has gone through.

A milestone for our country!

Four years of work. We made it.

For the lenders, this is financial close. For the minister, a milestone. For the developer, the end of years of work.
Five years on, demand has grown more slowly than the plan assumed, and cheaper capacity has come online.

We are paying for energy we do not need, in a currency we do not earn.

And our customers pay tariffs that do not cover our costs.

The arrears have built up. Now the guarantee is called, and it lands on the national budget.

The lenders checked that they will be repaid. Who checked that the system can carry this for twenty years?

That test is ours. And today, no one applies it.

This project is stuck in the reform gap. It needs more credit enhancement.

Every guarantee we add lands on the budget. I see a liability trap.

Each side is right about its own quadrant. Without the second test, neither can tell which quadrant a particular project is heading for.

Before we sign: has it passed both tests?

The lender's test, yes. We can finance it.

And the state's test. Finance has stressed the largest call on the budget. It fits.

The grid can take the output on the commissioning date.

It is written down, and ready to publish.

Then we sign, and we publish the state's answer.

Why a power deal that lenders will finance has passed only half its examination
EMMANUEL BOUJIEKA KAMGA
FACT
A composite case: 120 MW,
financial close after four years of negotiation.
Source: the chapter's composite case, not a single transaction
FACT
How the deal was made bankable
CAPACITY IN US$The utility pays for the plant's capacity in US dollars,whether or not it takes the energy.
A GUARANTEEA partial risk guarantee stands behind the utility's payments.
By every standard that lenders apply, the project is sound.
RED TEAM
The plant runs. The lenders are repaid.
The sponsors earn their return.
What failed was something no one in the signing room had been asked to check.
DECISION
Every power project must pass two examinations
THE LENDER'S TESTCan the project be financed?
THE STATE'S TESTCan the power system and the public purse carry it for the life of its contract?
01
WHAT LENDERS
MEAN BY BANKABLE
Bankable: prudent lenders, after full due diligence,
are prepared to lend on terms that reach financial close.
A judgement by those who provide the debt, over the life of that debt, about being repaid.
FACT
The lender's questions
REVENUESecured by contract, and large enough to service the debt?
BUYERWill the buyer pay, and can it?
RISKSConstruction, operating and resource risks held by parties able to bear them?
STEP-INCan the lenders step in if the project company fails?
SPONSORSExperienced and adequately capitalised?
FACT
2–3×
the cost of capital for utility-scale clean energy in Africa, at least, compared with advanced economies
Source: CLDP and ALSF 2024 (Power Africa handbook)
FACT
Lenders pricing risk at that level want protection
CAPACITY CHARGETake or pay: paid for availability, not for energy dispatched
HARD CURRENCYThe tariff is indexed to a hard currency
BACKSTOPSovereign guarantee, letter of credit or multilateral partial risk guarantee
TERMINATIONDebt repaid in full if the contract ends early
RED TEAM
Bankability is achieved largely
by relocating risk, not removing it.
RED TEAM
Weak demand. A weaker currency. A buyer that stops paying.
The risk passes to the utility, its customers,
and in the end, the state.
The lender's test is passed because someone else agreed to carry what the lender will not.
DECISION
Not a criticism of lenders.
The difficulty: in most African power markets, no test of equal rigour is applied for those who receive the risk.

DECISION
What this book adds
A CHANGE OF ANGLEA weak buyer and a heavy fiscal burden are not only obstacles to bankability,but also consequences of it, when projects close on terms those weaknesses made possible.
A CHANGE OF LEVELThe state's test, applied to each transaction before signature, whatever its origin,and the result published.
A CHANGE OF EVIDENCEOne project per Mission 300 compact country, chosen by a rule that ignores the outcome,so stalled projects are studied too, and closed ones followed into operation.

DECISION
Each quadrant calls for a different response
SUSTAINABLE CLOSESpeed: delay has a real price in unserved demand and diesel
REFORM GAPWork on the system: tariffs, arrears, procurement, credit enhancement sized to what the state can afford
LIABILITY TRAPRestructure before signature: smaller plant, lighter take or pay, local currency, or no contract
MoU GRAVEYARDDiscipline: letting a weak MoU lapse costs little

05
SEVEN DIMENSIONS,
TWO QUESTIONS
DECISION
Seven dimensions, two questions (1 to 4)
DIMENSION
THE LENDER ASKS
THE STATE MUST ASK
1 · Need and least cost
Is there a market for the output?
Is this the cheapest way to meet a need the plan has identified?
2 · Grid
Can the plant connect, and is it paid if the grid fails?
Can the grid take the output without curtailment or payment for energy never delivered?
3 · Buyer and revenue
Will the buyer pay, or will someone pay for it?
Do tariffs and collections fund the contract without new subsidy?
4 · Fiscal exposure
Is there a sovereign backstop?
What is the largest call the budget could face, and does it fit the debt framework?
Source: author · Table 2.2
DECISION
Seven dimensions, two questions (5 to 7)
DIMENSION
THE LENDER ASKS
THE STATE MUST ASK
5 · Contract and risk allocation
Has risk been moved away from the project?
Is each risk held by the party able to manage it at least cost?
6 · Sponsor and process
Is the sponsor credible?
Was the project selected competitively, against the plan?
7 · Financing structure
Can the debt and equity be raised?
Does the structure add currency or refinancing risk that the state will carry?
Source: author · Table 2.2
FACT
“Power plants do not function in a vacuum”
CLDP and ALSF 2024 · behind the grid dimension
DECISION
The framework's own contribution
FISCAL EXPOSUREA transaction test, before signature,not a sector review once arrears appear.
THE STATE'S QUESTIONAsked on every dimension
TWO OUTCOMESTested against two outcomes, not one
FACT
The two outcomes
OUTCOME
WHAT IT MEASURES
INDICATORS
A · Financial close
Whether, and how quickly, the project passed the lender's test
Close reached or not; time from first public record to close
B · Distress after commissioning
Whether the project later failed the state's test
Persistent arrears; renegotiation; guarantee called; capacity paid for but not used
Source: author · Table 2.3
DECISION
Most evaluations stop at outcome A.
Outcome B asks whether that success lasted, and at whose expense.
FACT
One project per Mission 300 compact country,
chosen by a rule fixed before any coding.
Coded from public sources only. Where a country has no qualifying project, that absence is a finding.
RED TEAM
Five limits, stated at the outset
1A small sample: structured, focused comparison, not statistical inference
2Failures leave thinner records than successes
3Much of what the second test needs is not public
4Outcome B needs time: recent projects are 'not yet observable'
5It diagnoses; it does not rate named projects
DECISION
Who must be in the room before a deal is signed
MINISTRIES OF FINANCEA formal role before any PPA with take or pay or state support,backed by a stressed estimate of the largest call on the budget.
REGULATORS & PLANNERSConfirm the project fits the least-cost plan,and that the grid can take its output on the commissioning date.
DEVELOPMENT FINANCESize credit enhancement to what the state can carry,not only to what lenders require.
A BANKABLE PROJECT HAS PASSED ONLY HALF ITS EXAMINATION.
The other half: can the system and the state carry it for the life of the contract?
Both answers yes, written down and published, before signature.
